Got a Government Job? Money Lessons for New Employees

2 min readBeginnerPunjab Police Sub InspectorPSSSBgovernment jobmindset
Quick answer

Most of us are financially illiterate and spend more than we earn. Simple money habits every new government employee should build from salary one.

≈ 2 min to finish · Beginner

On the podcast I said something that surprised a few people: most of us are financially illiterate. Look around your village or city and I would guess 90–95% of people do not know how to manage, invest and spend the money they earn. A government job gives you a steady salary. It does not teach you what to do with it.

This is general learning from books and life, not investment advice. For decisions about your own money, speak to a qualified advisor.

The trap I see most often

Everyone knows what their salary is. Then they spend more than that: a new bike on EMI, a phone on EMI, functions, gifts. A few months later, a part of every salary is already gone before it arrives. That is the debt trap, and it catches people with good jobs too.

Five habits to build from the first salary

1. Pay yourself first. Decide a fixed share to save the day the salary comes, before you spend anything. The amount matters less than doing it every month.

2. Build an emergency fund. Keep a few months of expenses aside for illness, family needs or surprises, so that one bad month does not push you into a loan.

3. Separate needs from wants. Before any big purchase, wait a week. Most wants disappear; needs stay.

4. Be very careful with loans and EMIs. A loan for a home or education can make sense. A loan for something you want to show off rarely does.

5. Learn before you invest. Do not put money anywhere because a colleague or a reel said so. Understand what it is, the risk, and how you will get the money back.

Books that taught me this

  • The Richest Man in Babylon: the simplest rules on saving and growing money, through short stories. My favourite money book.
  • The Psychology of Money: why behaviour matters more than intelligence with money.
  • Rich Dad Poor Dad: changes how you look at income, assets and spending.
  • Think and Grow Rich: about goals and the mindset behind building wealth.

More on these in 5 Non-Syllabus Books Every Aspirant Should Read.

For aspirants still preparing

Start learning this now. When the job comes, you will already have a plan for the first salary instead of learning from mistakes.

Straight answers

Frequently asked questions

What should I do with my first government salary?

Before spending, decide a fixed amount to save every month, build an emergency fund and avoid taking loans for things you want rather than need. Learn the basics before choosing any investment.

Which books help with money management?

The Richest Man in Babylon, The Psychology of Money and Rich Dad Poor Dad are good starting points. They are about habits and thinking, not stock tips.
